issue.issue_text: Whether the assistance of Hanamant Bhimappa Reddi (PW-24) in drafting the complaint puts its credibility into question.

facts: The complainant (PW-1) was illiterate and could not read or write.
An advocate, Hanamant Bhimappa Reddi (PW-24), was summoned to draft the complaint on behalf of PW-1.
PW-1 affixed his thumb impression to the complaint drafted by PW-24.
The defense argued that having an advocate draft the complaint cast doubt on its credibility and the prosecution's case.
application: The Supreme Court reasoned that the role of the advocate (PW-24) in drafting the complaint could not be viewed negatively simply because he was a professional who paid attention to detail.
The Court noted that since the complainant (PW-1) was illiterate, it was logical for him to require assistance in writing the complaint.

The Court considered that any minor discrepancies in the drafting process were not significant enough ("not so stark") to undermine the case, especially given the short time frame in which the events occurred.

Crucially, the Court found that the core of the prosecution's case was not shaken because the defense had admitted their presence at the scene of the crime, and independent witnesses had assigned specific roles to each of the accused.
The Court explicitly asked and answered the question of whether the advocate's involvement cast doubt on the prosecution's case, concluding that it did not.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, holding that the assistance of an advocate (PW-24) in drafting the complaint for the illiterate complainant (PW-1) did not undermine its credibility. The Court found it logical for an illiterate person to need help, and it viewed the advocate's attention to detail as a neutral, not negative, factor. Furthermore, it concluded that the core of the prosecution's case remained strong due to other evidence, such as the accused admitting their presence at the scene.

issue.issue_text: Whether the discrepancy in the time of entrustment of the FIR to PW-28 dislodges the statement made in the examination-in-chief.

facts: There was a discrepancy regarding the time the First Information Report (FIR) was entrusted to PW-28.
The statement in the examination-in-chief mentioned the time as 4:45 p.m.
This was contrasted with the general working hours, which were stated as 8 a.m. to 8:00 p.m.
law: A discrepancy or delay in procedural matters, such as the handling of an FIR, is not automatically fatal to the prosecution's case.
To successfully challenge a case based on such a discrepancy or delay, the accused must demonstrate that they have suffered prejudice as a result.
application: The Supreme Court affirmed the High Court's view, which was based on a full appreciation of all the evidence on record.
The Court held that this specific time discrepancy was not significant enough to discredit or "dislodge" the statement made by the witness during the examination-in-chief.
The Court noted that while the defense raised the issue, they failed to make any submission showing how this discrepancy caused any prejudice to the accused.
The Court stated that arguments without adequate backing or demonstration of prejudice cannot influence its decision.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, concluding that the discrepancy in the time of entrustment of the FIR to PW-28 was not a sufficient reason to disbelieve the statement made in the examination-in-chief, especially since no prejudice to the accused was demonstrated.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the assistance of Hanamant Bhimappa Reddi (PW-24) in drafting the complaint puts its credibility into question.
appellant_arguments: The credibility of the complaint is doubtful because it was drafted by an advocate (PW-24) and not by the complainant (PW-1) himself, who is illiterate.
There is a discrepancy as to whether the complaint was drafted based on the instructions of PW-1 or on notes prepared by the police, which shakes the genesis of the prosecution's case.
respondent_arguments: The role of PW-24, an advocate, in drafting the complaint should not be viewed negatively, as his profession means he would pay attention to detail.
The complainant (PW-1) stated he does not know how to read and write, making it necessary for someone else to write the complaint for him.
Any discrepancy in the drafting process is not significant enough to cast doubt on the prosecution's case, especially given the short time frame in which the events occurred.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: When appellants challenge concurrent findings of fact from lower courts, the burden is on them to establish special circumstances or an equally probable version of facts, and the prosecution is not required to prove specific acts committed by specific persons when the presence of the accused is not disputed.
obiter: This Court has on numerous occasions considered cases similar in nature, and, from such consideration emanated various principles in deciding the cases.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Court found no merit in the appeals, holding that under its limited jurisdiction in Article 136, it will not interfere with concurrent findings of fact from lower courts except in very special circumstances. Since the case rests on direct evidence, the presence of the accused was undisputed, and the legal principles concerning interested witnesses and group liability were correctly applied, there were no gross errors or crying circumstances to justify overturning the conviction.
legal_tests_applied: Standard of Review for Concurrent Findings of Fact: The Supreme Court will not interfere with concurrent findings of fact from lower courts unless there are "very special circumstances," a "gross error," the overlooking of "crying circumstances," or a misapplication of "well established principles of criminal jurisprudence."

Group Liability under Masalti: In cases of group crime where the number and presence of the accused are not disputed, the prosecution is not required to prove specific acts attributable to each specific person.

Credibility of an Interested Witness: The testimony of a witness who is a close relative of the deceased cannot be rejected on that ground alone, as there is no legal proposition that casts doubt on such a statement simply for that reason.
why_appellant_lost: The appellants failed to meet the high threshold for the Supreme Court to interfere with the concurrent findings of guilt from the two lower courts.
The argument that the sole eyewitness (PW-1) was an "interested witness" was rejected, as the court affirmed the principle that being a close relative is not a ground to reject testimony.

The court applied the landmark holding in 'Masalti', stating that with the number and presence of the accused being undisputed, the prosecution did not need to prove specific acts by each individual accused to secure a conviction for the group.
The appellants failed to establish the existence of special circumstances or an equally probable version of facts to counter the direct evidence presented by the prosecution.
why_respondent_won: The prosecution's case was based on direct evidence, not circumstantial evidence, which was upheld by two separate courts.

The conviction was supported by established legal principles, including the reliability of a single eyewitness (even a relative) and the doctrine of group liability where individual acts need not be proven.
The concurrent findings of the trial court and the High Court created a strong presumption in favor of the prosecution's case, which the appellants were unable to dislodge.
policy_considerations: A mechanical rejection of an even “partisan” or “interested” witness may lead to a failure of justice.

The Court exercises restraint in its power under Article 136, declining to interfere with lower court findings merely because it might have arrived at a different conclusion, thereby upholding the hierarchy and finality of the judicial process absent compelling errors.
